title: Week 15 · Lesson 39: Gastrointestinal Pharmacology — Acid Suppression, Antiemetics & Bowel Medication Safety
html:
PHASE 2 · ADVANCED PHARMACOLOGY

Week 15 — Lesson 39: Gastrointestinal Pharmacology — Acid Suppression, Antiemetics & Bowel Medication Safety

FNP-level goal: Match gastrointestinal symptoms to mechanism-based medication choices while recognizing alarm features, adverse effects, interactions, and presentations that should not be managed as routine outpatient GI disease.

Learning Objectives

  • Differentiate antacids, H2-receptor antagonists, proton pump inhibitors (PPIs), and potassium-competitive acid blockers by therapeutic role.
  • Use alarm features and a focused differential before empiric acid suppression.
  • Apply a safe, indication-based approach to PPI reassessment and de-prescribing.
  • Recognize antiemetic adverse effects, including sedation, anticholinergic burden, and QT-risk context.
  • Choose constipation and diarrhea medications only after considering obstruction, infection, inflammatory disease, and medication causes.
  • Identify urgent GI presentations requiring emergency evaluation or specialist involvement.

Part 1 — Do Not Treat “Stomach Symptoms” as One Diagnosis

Heartburn, epigastric pain, nausea, bloating, constipation, diarrhea, and abdominal pain are symptom clusters—not diagnoses. GERD, peptic ulcer disease, medication injury, H. pylori infection, biliary disease, pancreatitis, ischemia, malignancy, bowel obstruction, inflammatory bowel disease, infection, pregnancy, and disorders of gut-brain interaction can overlap.

Before selecting medication, ask: What syndrome is most likely? What would make it dangerous? Is the patient stable, hydrated, and able to take oral medication? Medication should follow diagnostic reasoning, not replace it.

Part 2 — Dyspepsia, Reflux, and Cardiac Safety

Retrosternal burning may be GERD, but pressure, nausea, or “indigestion” can also represent acute coronary syndrome—especially with exertion, dyspnea, diaphoresis, radiation, syncope, or cardiovascular risk factors. Acid suppression must never delay emergency evaluation of potentially ischemic chest symptoms.

For upper-GI symptoms, assess timing with meals, recumbency, dysphagia, odynophagia, NSAID exposure, alcohol, tobacco, anticoagulants, weight change, vomiting, anemia symptoms, and GI bleeding. These details change both medication choice and disposition.

Part 3 — Acid Suppression: Different Mechanisms, Different Uses

Antacids neutralize existing gastric acid and can provide short-term symptom relief. They may interfere with absorption of other medications and can create electrolyte or kidney-related concerns depending on ingredients and patient context.

H2-receptor antagonists reduce acid secretion through histamine-2 receptor blockade. They can be useful in selected patients, but indication, renal function, interactions, and symptom pattern still matter.

PPIs suppress gastric acid more strongly by inhibiting the gastric proton pump. They are important therapies for appropriate indications such as selected GERD and ulcer-related conditions. They are not a diagnostic label, a treatment for unexplained weight loss, or a substitute for evaluation of alarm features.

Part 4 — PPIs: Prescribe an Indication, Not an Autopilot Refill

For each PPI prescription, document the intended indication, expected treatment strategy, reassessment plan, and patient-specific risk factors. Technique matters: the patient should understand the prescribed timing and the reason it is being used. A patient who says a PPI “failed” may have an adherence, timing, diagnostic, or ongoing-trigger problem rather than a need for indefinite escalation.

Patients on long-term PPIs should have their indication periodically reviewed. Some patients have clear reasons to continue therapy; others may be candidates for a supervised step-down or discontinuation trial. Do not stop an appropriate PPI solely because of fear generated by a list of associations. Consider the underlying condition and upper-GI bleeding risk first.

Part 5 — Rebound Symptoms and PPI De-Prescribing

After stopping a long-term PPI, transient rebound acid hypersecretion can occur. Explain this possibility before changing the plan so the patient does not interpret rebound symptoms as proof that they must resume indefinite therapy without reassessment.

De-prescribing is not appropriate for every patient. Complicated erosive disease, peptic stricture, Barrett’s esophagus, eosinophilic esophagitis, high upper-GI bleeding risk, and other specific contexts may change the risk-benefit assessment. Use current guidance and specialty input when the indication is uncertain or high risk.

Part 6 — NSAIDs, Ulcer Risk, and Medication Reconciliation

NSAIDs can injure gastroduodenal mucosa and increase ulcer or bleeding risk, especially with older age, prior ulcer/GI bleed, corticosteroids, anticoagulants, antiplatelets, kidney disease, alcohol exposure, and multiple NSAID products. “Over-the-counter” does not mean low-risk.

Ask specifically about ibuprofen, naproxen, aspirin-containing products, combination cold medications, and topical/oral pain treatments. The FNP should define the indication, duration, alternatives, bleeding-risk context, and gastroprotection strategy when clinically appropriate rather than simply adding a PPI to an unsafe medication pattern.

Part 7 — H. pylori and Ulcer Reasoning

H. pylori testing and treatment strategies are diagnosis- and region-specific. Do not treat nonspecific dyspepsia with a memorized antibiotic combination without confirming the clinical question, allergies, prior antibiotics, local resistance context, drug interactions, and a plan to confirm eradication when indicated.

GI bleeding, anemia, persistent vomiting, severe pain, perforation concern, or hemodynamic instability requires urgent evaluation—not outpatient trial-and-error eradication therapy.

Part 8 — Nausea and Vomiting: Symptom Relief Cannot Replace the Differential

Antiemetics may improve nausea while a dangerous cause continues. Pregnancy, medication toxicity, migraine, vestibular disease, gastroenteritis, bowel obstruction, pancreatitis, hepatitis, DKA, increased intracranial pressure, sepsis, and myocardial ischemia are only some possible causes.

Assess duration, oral intake, hydration, urine output, pregnancy possibility, severe headache, abdominal pain, distention, fever, chest symptoms, neurologic findings, diabetes, recent medication changes, and substance exposure before simply sending an antiemetic prescription.

Part 9 — Antiemetic Medication Safety

Antiemetic classes have different risks. Some can cause sedation, falls, confusion, anticholinergic effects, extrapyramidal symptoms, or drug interactions. Some can contribute to QT prolongation, especially in patients with electrolyte abnormalities, congenital QT risk, bradycardia, structural heart disease, or concurrent QT-prolonging medication exposure.

For an older adult with polypharmacy, a patient with syncope or palpitations, or a patient with vomiting-related electrolyte loss, the question is not simply, “Which antiemetic works?” It is, “Which option is safest in this clinical context, and does the patient need urgent evaluation instead?”

Part 10 — Constipation: First Exclude the Dangerous Causes

Constipation can result from low fiber or fluid intake, immobility, pregnancy, diabetes, hypothyroidism, neurologic disease, opioid use, iron, calcium-channel blockers, anticholinergics, and many other medications. New severe constipation with abdominal distention, vomiting, severe pain, inability to pass flatus, fever, GI bleeding, or systemic illness raises concern for obstruction, ileus, volvulus, ischemia, or another urgent condition.

Do not reflexively prescribe multiple laxatives before assessing the patient’s baseline bowel pattern, medication causes, hydration, abdominal examination, and red flags.

Part 11 — Constipation Medications: Match the Agent to the Problem

Fiber can help selected patients, but rapid escalation in a poorly hydrated patient or one with possible obstruction may worsen symptoms. Osmotic agents such as polyethylene glycol can be useful for chronic idiopathic constipation in appropriate patients. Stimulant laxatives may have a role as short-term or rescue therapy. Prescription secretagogues and prokinetic options may be considered after an individualized evaluation and appropriate trials.

Magnesium-containing products require caution in kidney disease. Bowel regimens should include a follow-up plan: expected effect, adverse effects, hydration guidance, stop/call thresholds, and reassessment if constipation persists or changes.

Part 12 — Opioid-Induced Constipation Is a Medication Adverse Effect

Opioids reduce GI motility and can cause clinically important constipation. Do not wait for impaction or an ED visit to ask about bowel function. Start prevention and monitoring when clinically appropriate, reassess the ongoing opioid indication, and distinguish uncomplicated constipation from obstruction or impaction.

Some patients need targeted therapies beyond routine laxatives, but these decisions require medication reconciliation, renal/hepatic context, cost review, and an assessment for red flags.

Part 13 — Diarrhea: Treat Volume and Cause Before Suppressing Motility

Acute diarrhea may be infectious, medication-related, inflammatory, ischemic, endocrine-related, malabsorptive, or functional. The first medication may be oral rehydration and electrolyte support—not an antimotility agent.

Fever, bloody stool, severe abdominal pain, peritoneal signs, dehydration, hypotension, altered mental status, recent hospitalization/antibiotics, immunocompromise, or suspected inflammatory/invasive infection changes the plan. In those contexts, do not casually suppress motility; evaluate the cause and urgency.

Part 14 — Antidiarrheals and Bismuth: Safety Context Matters

Antimotility therapy can be reasonable for selected noninvasive, uncomplicated diarrhea, but it is not appropriate in every infectious or inflammatory presentation. Bismuth-containing products have their own interactions and patient-specific considerations. Ask about anticoagulants, salicylate sensitivity, kidney disease, pregnancy, fever, blood in stool, and recent antibiotic exposure.

Diarrhea with tachycardia, orthostasis, low urine output, confusion, or inability to maintain oral intake is a volume-status problem and may need urgent in-person treatment.

Part 15 — IBD, IBS, and the Danger of Anchoring

IBS is a diagnosis made after appropriate assessment, not a label for unexplained alarm features. Unintentional weight loss, nocturnal symptoms, anemia, blood in stool, family history suggesting higher risk, persistent fever, or a new change in bowel pattern in an older patient requires a broader workup.

Inflammatory bowel disease therapies can involve immunosuppression, infection screening, laboratory monitoring, and specialist coordination. Do not initiate complex IBD medication strategies as a substitute for establishing the diagnosis and referral pathway.

Part 16 — GI Medication Interactions Often Start Outside the Prescription List

Calcium, iron, magnesium, herbal products, alcohol, cannabis, antacids, laxatives, antidiarrheals, NSAIDs, and acid-suppressing drugs can all affect symptoms, medication absorption, kidney function, bleeding risk, or diagnostic interpretation. Ask what the patient actually takes on a typical day.

Medication reconciliation is especially important when a patient has nausea, diarrhea, constipation, unexplained anemia, recurrent reflux, CKD, anticoagulant therapy, pregnancy potential, or polypharmacy.

Part 17 — Clinical Case: “Reflux” With Alarm Features

A 62-year-old reports progressive dysphagia, early satiety, 12-pound unintentional weight loss, and fatigue. They request a stronger PPI.

The FNP response is not routine dose escalation. Dysphagia + weight loss + possible anemia are alarm features that require prompt diagnostic evaluation and appropriate referral. Acid suppression may be part of a plan, but it must not delay investigation.

Part 18 — Clinical Case: Vomiting and QT Risk

A patient with vomiting has palpitations, poor intake, and takes several medications with QT-prolongation potential. They request an antiemetic refill.

Build the mechanism: vomiting → possible potassium/magnesium loss → altered repolarization reserve; concurrent QT-active medications → greater arrhythmia risk. Assess stability, ECG/laboratory needs, drug interactions, and the cause of vomiting before selecting symptomatic therapy.

Part 19 — Clinical Case: “Just Constipation”

An 80-year-old using opioids presents with four days of no bowel movement, progressive abdominal distention, vomiting, and inability to pass flatus.

This is not a routine laxative refill. Distention + vomiting + obstipation raises concern for obstruction, ileus, or impaction and requires urgent evaluation.

FNP Gastrointestinal Medication Framework

  1. Name the symptom syndrome and identify alarm features before choosing a medication.
  2. Assess stability, hydration, bleeding risk, pregnancy possibility, and ability to take oral medication.
  3. Choose therapy for a defined mechanism and indication.
  4. Review NSAIDs, anticoagulants, OTC products, supplements, alcohol, and recent medication changes.
  5. Plan dose timing, expected response, adverse-effect monitoring, and reassessment or de-prescribing when appropriate.
  6. Escalate for bleeding, obstruction, peritoneal signs, severe dehydration, progressive dysphagia, unexplained weight loss, or possible cardiac/other systemic emergency.

High-Yield Summary

PPIs: are valuable for appropriate indications; regularly reassess the ongoing reason for chronic therapy.
GERD-like symptoms: do not exclude cardiac ischemia or GI alarm pathology.
Antiemetics: require sedation, anticholinergic, interaction, and QT-risk assessment.
Constipation: first exclude obstruction and medication causes; match therapy to mechanism.
Diarrhea: prioritize volume status and cause before suppressing motility.
Alarm features: bleeding, progressive dysphagia, weight loss, severe pain, distention/vomiting, dehydration, or instability change disposition.

Clinical safety note: This lesson is educational. GI diagnosis, medication selection, dosing, H. pylori treatment, PPI de-prescribing, bowel regimens, antiemetic use, and referral must follow current guidelines, prescribing information, local scope requirements, and the individual patient’s clinical context.
